    Content from The eLabFTW API

    Last updated on 2026-11-12 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What is a (REST) API?
    • What can I do with the eLabFTW API
    • Where can I find help on the eLabFTW API
    • How can I write and API call?
    • How can I view the response?

    Objectives

    • explain what a (REST) API is (in very basic terms)
    • explain what they can do with the eLabFTW API
    • find help on the eLabFTW API
    • formulate the API URL for a given eLabFTW instance
    • make a basic eLabFTW API call using the browser
    • interpret eLabFTW API responses

    Introduction to APIs

    In this course, we will be using the eLabFTW API to interact with the ELN. First, though, let’s take a step back and clarify what APIs are.

    API is short for application programming interface. You may also see the term REST or RESTful API, which indicates that an API conforms to design principles of the representational state transfer (REST) architectural style.

    An API, or application programming interface, is a set of rules or protocols that enables software applications to communicate with each other to exchange data, features and functionality. (https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/api)

    A (REST) API is, simply put, something that allows you to (programmatically) interface an application.

    Let’s use an analogy from the real world: a restaurant.

    Restaurant | Software:

    • In a restaurant, the guests want food, which the kitchen can provide.
    • In a software system, one application wants information that another can provide.

    Waiter | API:

    • In a restaurant, the waiter takes your order to the kitchen and brings back your food.
    • In software, the API receives your request and provides the appropriate response.

    Menu | Documentation:

    • In a restaurant, there is a menu that describes which food is available at which cost.
    • In software, the documentation describes what the API can provide and how.

    Kitchen | Server:

    • In a restaurant, there is the kitchen with its staff to provide food for guests.
    • In software, the server and its processes provide data to users.

    Table | Application:

    • In a restaurant, the guests sit at the table to interact with the food from the kitchen they get from the waiter.
    • In software, the user uses an application to work with data from a server provided by its API.

    The eLabFTW API

    Note: we’ve included a notepad in your workshop folder that has some useful things, such as links, to copy and paste.

    eLabFTW’s API let’s you interact with the ELN, e.g., retrieve and write information from it, without using the graphical user interface (GUI). This is something you may want to do to create automated workflows and avoid repetitive work.

    Sticking with our restaurant analogy, we first need to figure out what is available to us, in programmatic terms: what requests we may make (or in restaurant terms: what orders we may place).

    To this end, we head to the menu, or in the API’s case, the documentation, or short docs:

    This gives us very basic information on the API. If we scroll down we find another link to the full documentation.

    Two things are important for this course: (1) the HTML doc (v2) and (2) the Python Library (v2) link, the latter two of which we will get to later. The third, the version 2 documentation link, which leads to the APIs Swagger documentation page, which can also be helpful as a quick reference, however, we won’t be using it here.

    We will mainly focus on the to the HTML doc (v2). To the left, we have the various API methods allowed for each type of API, e.g. items (resources in the graphical user interface (GUI)), experiments, items, and so on.

    Scrolling through the categories and knowing how eLabFTW is structured, we can get a pretty good idea of the types of interaction we can carry out. For instance, under API METHODS - EXPERIMENTS we see there are options to delete, get, post, patch, and read.

    Selecting a methods gives us more information, e.g., we can see that postExperiments creates an experiment, as well as usage examples in different programming languages and the parameters we can give our API request.

    Looking at the description, a lot of this is similar to what we seen in the GUI: we have the body (main text), some permissions settings, category settings, and so on.

    On things to keep in mind is that, opposed to the GUI, we usually need to use an ID to indicate certain attributes. For example, we would not use the name of a category but it’s ID. One way to find these visually is in the address bar of our browser when we filter for certain attributes.

    Constructing Requests

    The first time you see these types of docs pages, it may seem a bit daunting. So let’s construct our first API call using a tool we’re all familiar with: our browser.

    First, just as a little reference, scroll all the way down to the USERS section on the HTML Docs page and select readUser. We can see the endpoint will be constructed to end with /users/{id}. If we look down at the parameters, we can also see that id may be set to me. In the usage example we can see how the request url will be formatted:

    "https://elab.local:3148/api/v2/users/{id}"

    Now, head to the browser:

    1. Write the eLabFTW URL, e.g., https://elab.parks.web.gateway.ionos.coscine.dev (match to your instance) in the menu bar.
    2. Add /api/v2.
    3. Add /users/me, behind this (hint: for more complicated endpoints, copy and paste from docs by hovering over the endpoint and using the clipboard icon).
    4. You show now have something that looks http://elab.parks.web.gateway.ionos.coscine.dev/api/v2/users/me.
    5. Hit return.

    If you are not logged in, you will get a 401 error since you are not authorized to view this information. Log in to eLabFTW, then refresh the page.

    Challenge

    API vs. UI

    What information are you shown? How does this information correlate to what you can see in the UI? What information is not included in eLabFTW’s GUI (for normal users).

    Most of the information can be find in the GUI. For example, the keyboard shortcut set in your user profile are:

    JSON 

    "sc_create": "c",
"sc_edit": "e",
"sc_favorite": "f",
"sc_todo": "t",
"sc_search": "s"

    In our user settings:

    Similarly, we can see our teams, which we can also see in our user profile, and so on.

    The top line has the userid attribute, which is your user ID. This piece of information is only really visible to team and system admin in the GUI (probably since it is not a useful piece of information in the GUI for day-to-day use).

    Requests typically return JSON. Depending on which browser you are using, it may be rendered nicely for better readability. Understanding the structure can greatly help when you are trying to find a specific piece of information. What helpful is knowing which key the value you are looking for belongs to. userid was the key in our example.

    We can also see a nested structure when we look at the teams key, with more keys provided for each team listed.

    Key Points
    • An API lets us interact with software in a programmatic manner
    • The APIs docs let us know which requests we may make
    • We can use the browser to make requests and view the response

    Attribution

    Content from The API in the Terminal

    Last updated on 2026-11-13 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What tools aside from the browser can I use to make API requests?
    • How can I authenticate myself?

    Objectives

    • Create an API token in the eLabFTW GUI
    • Make a basic call to the eLabFTW API using the command line and curl
    • Make user-specific API calls using the command line and curl and the API token

    Command-Line Interface

    Using our browser isn’t exactly useful when we want to automate workflows.

    A useful, built-in tool is a command-line interface, terminal, prompt, shell, and so on. The terminology is rather specific to operating system and often used interchangeably. We’re going to use terminal in the remainder of this course.

    Open a new terminal in Jupyter Lab. (Hint: if you already have a window open, use the blue + button in the top left corner of the Jupyter Lab window to open a new launcher. Then click the terminal icon.)

    We will use a tool called cURL to make API calls. This is a typical tool used for data transfer.

    We could head to its documentation to learn how to use it, but let’s be lazy and use what we already have, e.g., the usage examples in the HTML doc (v2) we just saw.

    Sticking to Users, let’s replicate what we did in our browser as a cURL request. You can try to construct this in your terminal, but for many of us it is easier in a text editor. Copy and paste the cURL code.

    Unlike our browser, through which we have been identified by logging in, we now need to tell the ELN we are allowed to have access. This is done by creating a token:

    1. Head your eLabFTW instance
    2. click your initials on the top right-hand side
    3. click settings
    4. Select the API KEYS header
    5. Under Create new key, enter a name for your key and select Read/Write from the permissions drop-down menu.
    6. click Generate an API Key
    7. Copy and paste this to the secrets.env file in your workshop_data/scripts/ folder for later use. It will only be shown once in the ELN’s GUI!

    Now we can start editing the request:

    1. Paste your token, replacing [[apiKey]]
    2. Replace https://elab.local:3148 with your eLabFTW URL
    3. Replace {id} with me
    4. Put spaces before the /
    Caution

    The cURL examples in the HTML Docs page are missing a white space before the backslashes (/). Whenever you copy-and-paste from here, you will have to add them.

    If you are working in the a text editor, copy this code into your terminal. Now, we will execute by hitting enter.

    Callout

    You can type this info directly into your terminal. For larger requests, however, especially when just starting out, it can be difficult to navigate. Thus, copy and pasting from a text editor may be easier and it is easier to catch problems.

    Callout

    You can load the API key from the secrets.env file instead of pasting the secret into the command.

    We’ve included a template in the workshop folder under scripts/. If you need to create one, it should look like this:

    BASH 

    ELAB_API_KEY='YOUR_TOKEN_HERE'
ELAB_API_HOST='https://elab.parks.web.gateway.ionos.coscine.dev/api/v2'

    To load them, from the workshop directory, run:

    BASH 

    set -a
source scripts/secrets.env
set +a

    This set -a turns the allexport option on, while set +a turns it off again. Alternative, you could set single variables with export MY_VAR=value without having to turn allexport on and off.

    The key and host is will now available as the $ELAB_API_KEY and $ELAB_API_HOST environment variable. Use it in the request like this:

    BASH 

    curl -i -X POST \
   -H "Authorization: $ELAB_API_KEY" \
   -H "Accept: application/json" \
   -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
   -d '{"title":"my api exp"}' \
   "$ELAB_API_HOST/experiments"

    This keeps the token out of the command itself. Do not print the variable or share the secrets.env file. If you believe you unsafely used an API key, always revoke it and create a new one.

    Note: .env is more common, however, Jupyter lab immediately hides these.

    Now, let’s make a new request and create an experiment:

    In the HTML Docs, Scroll to the Experiments section on the left and click postExperiment. Posting basically means we are creating something new, while patch, for example, would mean we are modifying something. Again, we will look at the cURL usage example and copy and paste it into our text editor. Similar to the steps above:

    1. Copy and paste your token to the terminal, replacing [[apiKey]]
    2. Replace https://elab.local:3148 with your eLabFTW URL
    3. Add experiment info using the template below. Once done, add \ at the end of the last line, enter for a new line and add -d '{"title":"my api exp"}' (replace info in curly brackets with the full data)
    4. Add -i (include) before -X (allows you to set HTTP method explicitly) in the top line. This ensures the response is output.
    5. Copy and paste into your terminal
    6. Hit enter to run

    Note: Don’t forget to add spaces between the \ and the end of the line.

    Template for data - find this in workshop_data/notepad.md:

    Feel free to modify!

    JSON 

    {
   "title": "Temperature calibration",
   "body": "<p>Calibration check for the temperature sensor before the measurement run.</p><p>Expected range: 20-25 degrees C.</p>",
   "canread_base": 30,
   "canwrite_base": 20,
   "canread": "{\"teams\": [], \"users\": [], \"teamgroups\": []}",
   "canwrite": "{\"teams\": [], \"users\": [], \"teamgroups\": []}",
   "category": 27,
   "metadata": {
      "extra_fields": {
         "sample_id": {
            "type": "text",
            "value": "TC-2026-001"
         },
         "instrument": {
            "type": "text",
            "value": "Omega HH506RA"
         },
         "run_number": {
            "type": "number",
            "value": 1
         },
         "target_temperature": {
            "type": "number",
            "value": 22
         },
         "calibration_status": {
            "type": "select",
            "value": "planned"
         }
      }
   }
}

    Final code:

    BASH 

    curl -i -X POST \
    -H "Authorization: $ELAB_API_KEY" \ 
    -H "Accept: application/json" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{
   "title": "Temperature calibration",
   "body": "<p>Calibration check for the temperature sensor before the measurement run.</p><p>Expected range: 20-25 degrees C.</p>",
   "canread_base": 30,
   "canwrite_base": 20,
   "canread": "{\"teams\": [], \"users\": [], \"teamgroups\": []}",
   "canwrite": "{\"teams\": [], \"users\": [], \"teamgroups\": []}",
   "category": 27,
   "metadata": {
      "extra_fields": {
         "sample_id": {
            "type": "text",
            "value": "TC-2026-001"
         },
         "instrument": {
            "type": "text",
            "value": "Omega HH506RA"
         },
         "run_number": {
            "type": "number",
            "value": 1
         },
         "target_temperature": {
            "type": "number",
            "value": 22
         },
         "calibration_status": {
            "type": "select",
            "value": "planned"
         }
      }
   }
}' \
   "https://elab.parks.web.gateway.ionos.coscine.dev/api/v2/experiments"

    If we run the code without the -i it will run all the same, but will not output any information.

    Callout

    Code pieces such as -i are called flags or options. Find out more in the cURL Documentation Man Page.

    Challenge

    Challenge

    What would the command line cURL API call look like that retrieves the experiment we just created? Write and execute this command. Then, analyze the response and see if everything is as you imagined.

    Look for the location in the response from your last call to get the ID.

    The POST response includes the URL of the new experiment in its Location header. Copy the experiment ID from that URL, then use it in a GET request:

    BASH 

    curl -X GET \
   -H "Authorization: $ELAB_API_KEY" \
   -H "Accept: application/json" \
   "$ELAB_API_HOST/experiments/<EXPERIMENT_ID>"

    This prints the JSON response directly in the terminal. The response should contain the experiment title and body, its creation and modification details, the permission settings, and the values in metadata.extra_fields.

    Callout

    If you have admin rights, for more readable, indented JSON, you can pipe the response through jq :

    BASH 

    curl -sS \
   -H "Authorization: $ELAB_API_KEY" \
   -H "Accept: application/json" \
   "$ELAB_API_HOST/experiments/<EXPERIMENT_ID>" | jq .

    Here, | passes the response to jq, and . tells jq to display the complete JSON document. If jq is not installed, install it with one of these commands:

    BASH 

    # macOS with Homebrew
brew install jq

# Debian or Ubuntu
sudo apt install jq

# Windows PowerShell with winget
winget install jqlang.jq

    On Windows PowerShell, use curl.exe rather than curl to call cURL explicitly, because curl may be an alias for a PowerShell command (shortened example):

    POWERSHELL 

    curl.exe ... | jq .
    Challenge

    Challenge

    The below code intends to link the device resource Bluetooth Infrared Thermometer to the experiment experiment created above.

    In it current state, it fails. What needs to be fixed?

    BASH 

    curl -X POST \
   -H "Authorization: $ELAB_API_KEY" \
   -H "Accept: application/json" \
   -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
   "https://elab.parks.web.gateway.ionos.coscine.dev/items/144/experiment/id"

    Read the docs for LinksToItems

    Assuming the token has been setup in the environment (or you have modified the code accordingly), the code was missing api/v2/ in the host url as well as the experiment id (modify with your id).

    BASH 

    curl -X POST \
   -H "Authorization: $ELAB_API_KEY" \
   -H "Accept: application/json" \
   -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
   "https://elab.parks.web.gateway.ionos.coscine.dev/api/v2/items/144/experiment/132"
    Key Points
    • API tokens authenticate requests made from the command line
    • cURL can create, retrieve, and update data through the eLabFTW API
    • API responses contain JSON data and HTTP headers that help interpret the result
    • Environment variables and .env (or secrets.env) files keep API credentials out of commands

    Content from Using the API with Python in Jupyter Notebooks

    Last updated on 2026-11-13 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What is Python?
    • What is basic Python syntax?
    • What is a Jupyter Notebook?
    • Where can I find Python examples for the eLabFTW API?

    Objectives

    • Write basic Python code
    • Install the eLabFTW Python package
    • Write and execute basic markdown and Python in Jupyter Notebooks
    • Find and reuse eLabFTW Python examples for API clients

    What is Python?

    Python is a high‑level, interpreted programming language that was created in the early 1990s by Guido van Rossum. It reads almost like plain English, which makes it especially attractive for people whose primary expertise is not computer science (e.g. biologists, chemists, physicists, engineers).

    When you run a Python script, the Python interpreter reads the source code line‑by‑line, translates it into byte‑code, and executes it on the fly – you do not need a separate compilation step.

    • Python gives you a clean, readable language that lets you focus on the scientific question rather than low‑level programming details.
    • Its extensive libraries let you go from raw data to publication‑quality figures in a few lines of code.
    • When performance becomes critical, you can combine Python with compiled extensions or off‑load heavy work to specialized tools.

    What is a Jupyter Notebook

    Let’s open a new Jupyter Notebook called ep_3_python_jupyter.ipynb. In Jupyter Lab, you can do this by clicking the blue + button, and then clicking the Python tile under notebook. Right-click the newly created notebook to and select rename to rename it.

    A Jupyter Notebook is an interactive web‑based document that combines executable code, rich text, plots, and multimedia in a single, linear layout. You open it in a browser, but the Python (or other language) kernel runs on your computer (or on a remote server) and evaluates each cell on demand. Core concepts

    • Cells – The notebook is divided into blocks called cells.

      • Code cells contain Python (or R, Julia, …) statements that are sent to the kernel when you press Shift + Enter. The output—text, tables, images, interactive widgets—appears directly below the cell.
      • Markdown cells hold formatted text written in Markdown (headings, lists, links, LaTeX equations, etc.). They let you annotate your analysis, describe the rationale, or document results.

    • Kernel – A background process that executes the code. The notebook UI sends the cell’s source to the kernel, receives the result, and displays it. You can restart, interrupt, or switch kernels (e.g., Python 3, R) without leaving the notebook.

    • Output – Anything that a normal read–eval–print loop (REPL) would print can appear: plain text, JSON, tables, Matplotlib/Plotly figures, HTML, LaTeX‑rendered equations, or interactive widgets (sliders, drop‑downs).

    Crash course: Python Basics

    1. Printing & basic data types

    PYTHON 

    # Print a greeting
print("Hello, eLabFTW researcher!")

# Numbers, strings, booleans, which can be stored in variables
my_int   = 42            # integer
my_float = 3.14          # floating‑point
my_bool  = True          # boolean

print(my_int, my_float, my_bool)

    Expected output

    Hello, eLabFTW researcher!
42 3.14 True

    2. Variables & dynamic typing

    PYTHON 

    a = 10          # a is an int
a = a * 2.5    # now a becomes a float (25.0)

print(a)

    Output

    25.0

    3. Lists (ordered collections)

    We can define lists of objects. They can be any type of data. For example strings (but they could also be mixed type).

    We can use indexing to retrieve items (starts at 0!), slice lists, and append new items.

    PYTHON 

    samples = ["S1", "S2", "S3"]   # create a list
print(samples[0])              # first element → "S1"
print(sample[2:3])             # slice, print part of list according to index

# Append a new sample name
samples.append("S4")
print(samples)

    Output

    S1
['S1', 'S2', 'S3', 'S4']

    4. Loop over a list (for‑loop) to create a dictionary

    We can iterate over a series, such as a list, to perform operations on each item. In this case, we have another data type, a dictionary, which is a collection of key:value pairs. We have a pattern where we:

    1. Initialize an empty dictionary, which is done with curly braces.
    2. Iterate over the sample list.
    3. Assign the key (sample) in the dictionary a value (the length pf the sample name string).

    PYTHON 

    results = {}
for sample in samples:
    results[sample] = len(sample)   # store the length of the name

print(results)

    Output

    {'S1': 2, 'S2': 2, 'S3': 2, 'S4': 2}

    5. Conditional statements

    Conditional statements give you the option to check a condition. In if-statements, if this condition is true, the indented code block will be varied out. An else-statement can be used in combination with an if to provide instructions on what to do if the if fails.

    PYTHON 

    threshold = 5
value = 7

if value > threshold:
    print("value is larger")
else:
    print("value is smaller or equal")

    Output

    value is larger

    6. Defining and calling a function

    Functions serve as reusable pieces of code. We define them using def:

    PYTHON 

    def check_value(value, threshold):
  if value > threshold:
    return "value is larger" 
  else:
    return "value is smaller or equal"

    Then we can call them using their name and passing any required parameters in parentheses:

    result = (check_value(7, 5))
print(result)

    Output

    'value is larger'

    Built-in Functions

    There are a number of built-in functions in Python, which means we don’t have to define everything ourselves. We’ve already seen some of these, for example, the print() function. Again, we call the function by it’s name and pass what it needs in the parentheses (as above print("Hello, eLabFTW researcher!")).

    The built-in function help() allows us to retrieve the documentation on functions, including built-in ones. For example, we can call help() on the built-in function type():

    PYTHON 

    help(print)

    Output

    Help on built-in function print in module builtins:

print(*args, sep=' ', end='\n', file=None, flush=False)
    Prints the values to a stream, or to sys.stdout by default.

    sep
      string inserted between values, default a space.
    end
      string appended after the last value, default a newline.
    file
      a file-like object (stream); defaults to the current sys.stdout.
    flush
      whether to forcibly flush the stream.

    Another useful built-in function is len() which gives is the length of things, such as, strings, lists, or dictionaries:

    PYTHON 

    len('Hello')

    Output

    5

    PYTHON 

    samples = ["S1", "S2", "S3"]   # create a list
len(sample)

    Output

    3

    See the Python Docs on built-in functions.

    Please note, we are working in a Jupyter Notebook and running text snippets. This is a great way to learn and explore data. If you were running automated scripts, you would write these in Python files, e.g., my_script.py which can be run in the terminal

    BASH 

    python my_script.py
    Challenge

    Challenge

    What will be printed?

    PYTHON 

    def add_five(value):
  return value + 5

result = add_five(5)
next_value = result + 1
print(result)

    A. 11
    B. 10
    C. TypeError

    B – The function adds 5 to the passed value of 5, returning the value of 10. This returned valued is stored in result and doesn’t change afterwards.

    The eLabFTW Python API Library

    One of the advantages of Python is that there are many ready-made libraries that allow us to easily reuse code others have created for a specific purpose.

    For eLabFTW, there is elabapi-python. We can find information on it via the API docs selection page by clicking Python Library (v2).

    Here, we can find some examples and information such as installation. We will do something similar to what the page says and install it directly via our Jupyter Notebook:

    BASH 

    %pip install elabapi-python
    Callout

    This installs it directly in the environment we are working in so it is accessible to our notebook.

    To install it locally (e.g., if you are working outside of the Jupyter environment), open a terminal window and install via pip. This usually looks like:

    BASH 

    pip install elabapi-python

    However, your Python and pip installation may use pip3 instead of pip.

    As indicated by the elabapi-python installation instructions, it is highly recommended to work in a virtual environment. We recommend uv for creating and managing these:

    BASH 

    cd workshop_data # change directory folder (if not already in this folder)
uv init --bare # initialize the project in the desired directory
uv add elabapi-python python-dotenv # add the API client and .env support
uv sync

    The package elabapi-python is imported as elabapi_python, and python-dotenv is imported as dotenv in client.py (we will get to that script in a minute). Ensure you have added your credentials and the URL to a .env (or secrets.env) file.

    Once downloaded, we need to import the library into our notebook or scripts:

    PYTHON 

    import elabapi_python

    Python does not allow dashes, therefore, this is replaced with an underscore when calling the library.

    To get basic help on any Python library in Jupyter, we can use the help() function. For example, to get help on the elabapi_python library, we can run:

    PYTHON 

    help(elabapi_python)

    Honestly, for this specific case, the help output is not extremely helpful. However, it does give us some information on the library. We can also use the dir() function to get a list of all the functions in the library:

    PYTHON 

    dir(elabapi_python)

    If we start the API docs again and click on Python Library (v2), we get are taking to a GitHub repository.

    Here, we have the examples folder on Github. This contains a nifty client configuration file. This has already been downloaded and included in your workshop_data directory. We have made some small adjustments to ensure the secrets load correctly.

    In the Python library, there are various clients that can be used to interact with the eLabFTW API. First, you set up the main one, which has already been done in client.py, then, you can create the others.

    We import the main api client into our notebook using:

    PYTHON 

    from scripts.client import api_client

    Note: ensure your are in the correct directory, workshop_data/.

    Callout

    When writing, you can avoid a lot of spelling errors by using tab to get suggestions.

    You may get an error here for missing packages, especially dotenv:

    PYTHON 

    %pip install python-dotenv

    Let’s look at a couple examples in the GitHub repo.

    Check out 00_getting-started.py. We can see an info client:

    PYTHON 

    info_client = elabapi_python.InfoApi(api_client)
api_response = info_client.get_info()
api_response
    Callout

    In Jupyter Notebooks, we often get a pretty printed output without using a print() statement. This only works for the last line of a cell, so if you want to see the output of multiple lines or when using in a script, you will need to use print().

    For example:

    PYTHON 

    api_response
4

    will output the number 4.

    As opposed to:

    PYTHON 

    print(api_response)
4

    which will output both api_response and the number 4.

    Back to the clients. We kind of see the pattern. We create a client for the methods we see in the HTML API Docs, and then use the method. We can do the exact same thing we did before and get our own user info:

    PYTHON 

    users_client = elabapi_python.UsersApi(api_client)
me = users_client.read_user('me') # alternative would be to use an ID
me

    Similarly, we can see an experiment client in the examples:

    PYTHON 

    exp_client = elabapi_python.ExperimentsApi(api_client)

    Check out line 87, which shows us how we retrieve an experiment. Remember how we created and retrieved an experiment in the terminal using cURL? Let’s try the same thing here using the experiment ID from the last lesson.

    PYTHON 

    exp_id = 94 # example; replace with your experiment ID
exp = exp_client.get_experiment(exp_id)
print(exp)

    You can see, this does the same things as we were doing before, but many of us find Python easier to read and understand than the terminal commands. This is especially true when we start to combine multiple steps into a single script.

    Challenge

    Challenge

    What is the code for the client that interacts with resources in eLabFTW? Create this client in your notebook and use it to:

    1. Retrieve all resources (you have access to) from your eLabFTW instance.
    2. Retrieve the bluetooth thermometer resource (from the last episode).

    Look through the examples and keep your eyes out for a different word than resources. We saw this in episode 01, as well.

    An example can be found in 05-create-modify-item in line 6:

    PYTHON 

    itemsApi = elabapi_python.ItemsApi(api_client)

    To retrieve and view all resources you have access to (1):

    PYTHON 

    resources = itemsApi.read_items()
resources # outputs the resource to the jupyter notebook

    To retrieve a specific resource (2):

    PYTHON 

    resource = itemsApi.get_item(144)
resource # outputs the resource to the jupyter notebook
    Key Points
    • Jupyter Notebooks combine executable Python code, Markdown, and output
    • Python variables, collections, loops, conditionals, functions, and JSON support basic data workflows
    • The elabapi-python package provides Python clients for the eLabFTW API
    • A configured API client can be reused to access information, experiments, and resources
    • API documentation and examples help identify the appropriate client and method

    Content from Working with Data from eLabFTW

    Last updated on 2026-11-13 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How can I retrieve experiment data with Python?
    • How can I access specific information within an experiment once I have retrieved it?
    • How can I upload files to eLabFTW with Python?
    • How can I start creating Python scripts for automated workflows between a local device and eLabFTW?

    Objectives

    • Retrieve an experiment from eLabFTW using Python
    • Access specific pieces of data from the information returned by the API
    • Perform bulk actions such as patching or uploading files to multiple experiments at once.

    Getting Experiment Parameters from eLabFTW

    In the previous episodes, we created an experiment, linked a resource, and showed how to retrieve ELN entries. Now, we will look at how to work with information from entries in eLabFTW.

    Here’s an overview of the intended workflow:

    ---
config:
  layout: fixed
accTitle: Schematic workflow for working with data from the ELN
---
flowchart

 subgraph s4["ELN (GUI)"]
        n3["Experiment"]
        n11["parameters (custom field metadata)"]
  end
 subgraph s3["Script"]
        n10["get parameters from ELN"]
        n6["output data files"]
        n5["run measurements"]
  end
 subgraph s2["Device Computer"]
        s3
  end
    n5 --> n6
    n6 -- attach --> n3
    n3 --> n11
    n10 --> n5
    n11 --> n10
    n12(["Researcher"]) -- plans --> n3

    To this end, head to our eLabFTW test instance via your in your browser. Create at least three experiments using the Heating Test template. Enter a different Laser Power value for each in the extra fields metadata. Note: You may change the title, just ensure the word ‘Heating’ remains.

    The configured client, which we worked with in the previous episode, loads the API host and token from the secrets.env or .env file beside client.py. Don’t forget to keep the token in the environment and do not place it in notebook cells or output - this is not as important if you are working on your personal computer, but is good to practice.

    With the experiments planned via the GUI, we now need to retrieve the parameters. To do so, we first retrieve the experiments, then we extract the information we need.

    Again, since we are using a new notebook we import everything we need:

    PYTHON 

    import elabapi_python
from scripts.client import api_client

    Note: run %pip install elabapi_python (or for any other packages) if needed.

    If we check the eLabFTW GUI for our own experiments, we will see our experiments with the category ‘MEASUREMENT’ with ‘Heating’ in the title:

    First, let’s get the experiments. To do so, we need the experiments api again. We also need a method to attach files. We can what that looks like by checking out the examples/03-experiment-file-handling.py in the github repository.

    We know we need the experiments API, let’s create it:

    PYTHON 

    experiments_api = elabapi_python.ExperimentsApi(api_client)
uploads_api = elabapi_python.UploadsApi(api_client)

    We could get all experiments, as we just saw in the previous episode, which would work fine for our little team, but is not really efficient in reality. Luckily, the API allows us to query and this filter what it returns.

    A quick check of the HTML eLabFTW API Docs for readExperiments gives us information here. You can query terms, look for experiments linked to specific other entries, and so on. We have a few options here, but let’s keep ot simple and look for experiments with status ‘Planning’ and ‘Heat’ in the title. We can get the status ID through the browser UI by filtering by the status and checking the address bar. We are also going to set the scope to only find our own experiments. From the docs we can see: 1: self, 2: team, 3: everything. It defaults to the user value stored in preferences. This ensures everyone is working with their own experiments.

    PYTHON 

    heating_experiments=experiments_api.read_experiments(q='Heating', status=80, scope=1)

    The return is a list of experiment objects. We can check how many it returned for a quick sanity check:

    PYTHON 

    len(heating_experiments)

    Output:

    3

    Note: if you created more, you list will be longer.

    We can access individual pieces of information from each of the returned experiments, which are elabapi-python objects. Let’s look at a single one and extract some information (remember how we can use indexing for lists, as shown in our crash course in episode 03):

    PYTHON 

    my_experiment = heating_experiments[0]
print(my_experiment.title)
print(my_experiment.created_at)
print(f"Experiment owned by: {my_experiment.fullname}")

    Output:

    Heating Test Run I
2026-10-30 09:55:43
Experiment owned by: Nicole Parks

    This is what we expect if we look at the same experiment in the GUI:

    Challenge

    Challenge

    How would you access the ID for each of the experiments you retrieved using the GUI?

    Bonus: How can you avoid having to access the experiment by its individual index each time you want to retrieve the ID?

    For bonus: Check out the previous episode on iteration

    You can use the same syntax as above to retrieve a an ID from a single experiment.

    PYTHON 

    heating_experiments[0].id

    We could then write

    PYTHON 

    print(heating_experiments[0].id)
print(heating_experiments[1].id)
print(heating_experiments[2].id)

    to print each id.

    To avoid having to access each individual one, we can use a for loop:

    PYTHON 

    for experiment in heating_experiments:
  print(experiment.id)

    What we need to run our experiments is the laser power entry. There’s a slight bug in the Python package as you may notice: the parameters, which would be in metadata are missing:

    PYTHON 

    print(my_experiment.metadata)

    Output:

    None

    This issue has been reported, but it has not been fixed, yet.

    The code for iterating over the experiments and pulling it out would be:

    PYTHON 

    power_settings = []
for exp in heating_experiments:
    power_setting = exp.metadata.extra_fields["Laser Power"]
    power_settings.append(power_setting)

    There’s many ways to get what we need: here, we will use the requests package to make the API request directly and get the full experiment information. The returned data structure is a bit different, but that’s fine.

    PYTHON 

    %pip install requests
from scripts.client import API_HOST, API_KEY
import requests

heating_experiments_full = []

for exp in heating_experiments:
    exp_id = exp.id
    endpoint = API_HOST + f'/experiments/{exp_id}'
    headers = {'Authorization': f'{API_KEY}'}
    response = requests.get(endpoint, headers=headers)
    heating_experiments_full.append(response.json())

    Generally, it’s good to know you have a lot of options to get where you need to be. Another possible workaround may have been, for example, to download the experiment as a JSON or ELN Format file and pull the info from there.

    Again we see all the information we would expect–and then some. Keeping our eyes out for the work metadata we see:

    'metadata': '{"extra_fields": {"Laser Power": {"type": "number", "unit": "W", "units": ["W"], "value": "50"}, "Switch-off Temperature": {"type": "number", "unit": "°C", "units": ["°C", "K"], "value": "100"}}}',
'metadata_decoded': {'extra_fields': {'Laser Power': {'type': 'number',
    'unit': 'W',
    'units': ['W'],
    'value': '50'},
  'Switch-off Temperature': {'type': 'number',
    'unit': '°C',
    'units': ['°C', 'K'],
    'value': '100'}}},

    Corresponding to the custom fields in our experiment:

    There is a metadata and a metadata_decoded. We can quickly check what te differences are by using Python’s built-in type() function. Note, values are accessed slightly differently in dictionaries than in elabapi-python objects:

    PYTHON 

    type(heating_experiments_full[0]['metadata'])

    Output:

    str

    PYTHON 

    type(heating_experiments_full[0]['metadata_decoded'])

    Output:

    dict

    Basically, metadata_decoded means the json-formatted string has already been decoded into a dictionary, which is easy to use in Python. This is what we need.

    Let’s output that part so we know how to access the values needed:

    PYTHON 

    heating_experiments_full[0]['metadata_decoded']

    Output:

    {'extra_fields': {'Laser Power': {'type': 'number',
   'unit': 'W',
   'units': ['W'],
   'value': '125'},
  'Switch-off Temperature': {'type': 'number',
   'unit': '°C',
   'units': ['°C', 'K'],
   'value': '100'}}}

    That means we can access each value accordingly:

    PYTHON 

    heating_experiments_full[0]['metadata_decoded']['extra_fields']['Laser Power']['value']

    Output:

    '125'

    We want to use hese in a pre-prepared script that contains a function that generates some synthetic data and saves it as a CSV (see scripts/generate_measurement.py). Let’s import this and run it for each experiment, e.g., every set of values. The function returns the path to the generated file, which we will save in a dictionary (with the experiment ID as the key) so we can easily access each one in later steps.

    PYTHON 

    from scripts.generate_measurement import generate_measurement

measurement_files = {}

for exp in heating_experiments_full:
    
    off_temp = exp['metadata_decoded']['extra_fields']['Switch-off Temperature']['value']
    
    laser_power = exp['metadata_decoded']['extra_fields']['Laser Power']['value']
    
    print(f"Running measurement with laser power {laser_power} and shut-off temperature {off_temp}...")
    
    out_path = generate_measurement(power_w = float(laser_power), break_temp = float(off_temp))
    
    print(f"Output file saved to {out_path}")
    measurement_files[exp['id']] = out_path

print(len(measurement_files))
measurement_files

    If you check the output folder output_data/, you will see three files have been created.

    Let’s go ahead and attach these back to the experiment. We can check line 42-47 in examples/23-create-resources-and-upload-pdfs.py in the GitHub Python examples to see how we upload files to entries.

    PYTHON 

    for exp in heating_experiments_full:
    exp_id = exp['id']
    power = exp['metadata_decoded']['extra_fields']['Laser Power']['value']
    for file in measurement_files:
        if file.name.startswith(power):
            uploads_api.post_upload(
                "experiments",
                exp_id,
                file=str(file),

    )

    If we check our experiments in the GUI, we should see your attached files:

    Challenge

    Challenge

    Write a for loops that sets each experiment status to running.

    Execute the code and check the GUI to see if it worked.

    Get an idea of what the commands could look like in the example examples/05-create-modify-item.py on GitHub.

    The request we are making is a patch to an existing experiment. We need to tell the

    PYTHON 

    for exp in heating_experiments_full:
    exp_id = exp['id']
    experiments_api.patch_experiment(exp_id, body={'status': 47})

    Note, and alternative using the original experiment return (using the elabapi-python package) would be:

    PYTHON 

    for exp in heating_experiments:
    exp_id = exp.id
    experiments_api.patch_experiment(exp_id, body={'status': 47})

    Here, we are working with the eLabFTW object instead of a dictionary, so we access the experiment ID differently.

    We could shorten this a bit:

    PYTHON 

    for exp in heating_experiments:
    experiments_api.patch_experiment(exp.id, body={'status': 47})
    Callout

    Showing this in a Jupyter Notebook helps you better understand the single steps. However, as you may have noticed, this is really innefficient, e.g. it loops over the experiments list and gets the power variable twice. This would all be consolidated into a script. Here, we would create single functions for each step and so on. Then this could be run automatically, e.g., on a device computer, maybe one schedule that checks for new experimets entered throug the GUI and then runs them for you and attached the output files for you to then check through the GUI.

    Key Points
    • Retrieve information using either the elabapi_python module or requests
    • Use queries and filters in your Python API requests
    • Access specific entries by given parameters in retrieved experiments
    • Iterate (loop) over lists of entries to perform bulk actions

    Data Analysis Workflows

    Let’s imagine we had used an automated workflow in episode 04 to create the files. Everything ran in our absence and we have the individual output files attached to the experiments.

    We can now keep going and add some more information to our experiments, such as a plot to quickly see the data, for example:

  layout: dagre

    We have not worked with Pandas or Matplotlib yet, but they are the most common Python libraries for data analysis and visualization. We will use them to load the CSV file and create a plot.

    Also note, we use aliases for certain libraries to make the code more concise. This is a common practice in Python, especially for frequently used libraries. pd is the standard alias for pandas.

    Since we’re in a new notebook, we set everything up by importing the package and creating the API clients we need:

    PYTHON 

    import elabapi_python
from scripts.client import api_client
experiments_api = elabapi_python.ExperimentsApi(api_client)
uploads_api = elabapi_python.UploadsApi(api_client)

    Let’s access one of our experiments and download the data file.

    We will continue to use the uploads_api to interact with attached files. To ensure we have our experiment information, let’s retrieve these again. We will filter by status again, but remember, we changed this to Running. The GUI reminds us that this status has ID 47.

    PYTHON 

    heating_experiments = experiments_api.read_experiments(q='Heating', status = 47, scope=1)

    Let’s work with a single experiment and retrieve the data file. This is where we need the ID from the retrieved experiments. We will work with the first one in our list.

    Check out the example in examples/03-experiment-file-handling.py.

    That gives us a function to work with. Let’s copy and paste and then modify slightly:

    PYTHON 

    experiment = heating_experiments[0]

def download_matching_uploads_locally(exp): # added experiment
    # display id, name and comment of the uploaded files and download them locally
    for upload in uploads_api.read_uploads('experiments', exp.id): # match uploads_api spelling
        print(upload.id, upload.real_name, upload.comment, upload.state)
        # get and save file
        with open(upload.real_name, 'wb') as file: # edited file name variable to match real name
            # the _preload_content flag is necessary so the api_client doesn't try and deserialize the response
            file.write(uploads_api.read_upload('experiments', exp.id, upload.id, format='binary', _preload_content=False).data) # edited exp.id, match uploads_api spelling

    This will download all files attached to the specified experiment. It does this by looping over the uploads, then using the uploads_api to read the file and write the file.

    After running the cell we can use the function.

    To call the it we write the name of the function, followed by parentheses, in which we pass the experiment in question:

    PYTHON 

    download_matching_uploads_locally(experiment)

    If we check our workspace, we can see the file has been downloaded.

    Callout

    The _preload_content=False argument is needed by this generated client when downloading file content. Without format="binary", the request returns upload information rather than the file itself.

    Visualize the Data

    Using pandas, we can easily read in and plot the data. First we import pandas. Again, We use the alias pd here, which is the standard way to import pandas. We read the CSV by file name using the read_csv method. Then, we can use head to view the first few lines of the dataframe.

    PYTHON 

    %pip install pandas # if needed
%pip install matplotlib # does not install automatically with pandas
import pandas as pd

measurement_data = pd.read_csv("50_measurement_2026-11-05T11:27:07.281399.csv")
measurement_data.head()

    Now, let’s create a quick plot. Pandas uses the package matplotlib to do this in a built-in manner.

    PYTHON 

    measurement_data.plot.scatter(x='time_s', y='temperature_C')

    This is very basic. Let’s add a title. We can also save he figure to a variable so we can keep working with it. In this case we want to save.

    PYTHON 

    ax = measurement_data.plot.scatter(x='time_s', y='temperature_C', title = 'Laser Power 50 W')

    We now have the plot with the title. You can make all kinds of changes here, from axis labels to colors, but for a quick overview, it’s sufficient. Let’s save it.

    PYTHON 

    ax.figure.savefig("50w_temp_time_plot.png", dpi=300)

    Attach to the experiment:

    PYTHON 

    uploads_api.post_upload('experiments', experiment.id, file="50w_temp_time_plot.png")
    Challenge

    Challenge

    Use the above snippets and function to write a code that

    1. Retrieves all run experiments
    2. Plots and saves figures for each
    3. Attaches the plot back to the experiment
    4. Sets the experiment status to success

    Bonus: If anyone can figure out how to add an image directly to the main text field using the API, please share!

    Make a small modification to the download_matching_uploads_locally so you can retrieve the file name.

    Here is one possible solution. This assumes you start with a new notebook or write a Python script, so it includes all data imports and retrieves the experiment information.

    PYTHON 

    import pandas as pd
import elabapi_python



def download_matching_uploads_locally(exp): 
    downloaded_file_names = [] # initialize empty list to collect file names
    for upload in uploads_api.read_uploads('experiments', exp.id): 
        print(upload.id, upload.real_name, upload.comment, upload.state)
        with open(upload.real_name, 'wb') as file: 
            file.write(uploads_api.read_upload('experiments', exp.id, upload.id, format='binary', _preload_content=False).data) 
        downloaded_file_names.append(upload.real_name) # add file name to list once downloaded
    return downloaded_file_names #return file name so we can access outside of function


heating_experiments = experiments_api.read_experiments(q='Heating', status = 47, scope=1) # retrieve experiment information with filters applied

for experiment in heating_experiments: # loop over each heating experiment in our list
    downloaded_file_names = download_matching_uploads_locally(experiment) # will download all files for each experiment we pass
    for file_name in downloaded_file_names: # loop over downloaded files

        if file_name.endswith('csv'): #make sure you're not trying to load some other type of file
            measurement_data = pd.read_csv(file_name) # load into dataframe
            power = file_name.split('_')[0] # get power setting from file name
            title = f"Laser Power {power} W" # dynamically set plot title
            ax = measurement_data.plot.scatter(x='time_s', y='temperature_C', title = title) # create plot
            figure_name = f"{power}w_temp_time_plot.png" # dynamically set figure name 
            ax.figure.savefig(figure_name, dpi=300) # save figure
            uploads_api.post_upload('experiments', experiment.id, file=figure_name) # upload figure file

    Challenge

    This is play time. Below are ideas of things you can try out. The solution provides hints rather than actual solutions for each point.

    • Change permissions on your create experiments
    • Book a device
    • Export entries in different formats
    • Create individual resources from a CSV (where each row represents a resource)

    Hints and places to start:

    • Change permissions on your create experiments: examples/14-fix-user-exp-permissions.py

    • Book a resource: examples/13-events.py, doc.elabftw.net/api/elabapi-html/#api-Events-postEvents

    • Export entries in different formats

      For ELN files:

      PYTHON 

      def download_eln_archive(
    experiment_id: int,
    download_folder: Path = Path("eln_downloads")
):
    """
    Download an experiment's ELN archive and save it to the specified folder.
    """
    # ensure the download folder exists
    download_folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    eln_file_path = download_folder / Path(f"{experiment_id}-export.eln")

    try:
        with open(eln_file_path, "wb") as file:
            response = experimentsApi.get_experiment(
                experiment_id, format="eln", _preload_content=False
            )
            file.write(response.data)
        logger.info(
            f"Downloaded ELN archive for experiment {experiment_id} to {eln_file_path}"
        )
        return eln_file_path
    except Exception as e:
        logger.error(
            f"Failed to download ELN archive for experiment {experiment_id}: {e}"
        )
        raise

    • Create individual resources from a CSV (where each row represents a resource) examples/09-import-csv.py

    If you would like to contribute your solutions, please don’t hesitate to do so. We can include them here for future courses.

    Key Points
    • The eLabFTW Python API client allows you to retrieve all or specific files attached to an experiment
    • Pandas can turn downloaded CSV data into a table ready for analysis
    • Pandas has built-in matplotlib plots to visualize data and save plots
